title: Jeff Nippard & Alec Enkiri Want Me To Deload... I Don't Wanna (Size vs Strength)
summary: A long response to deload videos by Alec Enkiri and Jeff Nippard, arguing that deload weeks are a powerlifting tool that does not suit maximalist bodybuilding. NH separates size and strength training, explains why bodybuilders autoregulate through sets and reps rather than load, and why muscle splits let fatigue clear without week-long breaks. He critiques the fitness-fatigue model and proposes performance minus fatigue equals fitness for bodybuilders.
claims: The current deload fashion on YouTube is powerlifting-centric and suits strength athletes far more than bodybuilders
Strength-focused lifters often treat hypertrophy as a by-product and bodybuilding as unworthy; bodybuilding is its own pursuit with its own methods
Bodybuilders spend more time in the gym because they do more reps, train more frequently and must cover more body parts, e.g. twice the direct biceps sets of a strength athlete
Strength training is effort-inducing; bodybuilding training is time-consuming and volume-targeted
He trains with high volume because his body responds better to volume; individuals skew toward responding to volume or intensity, and some of his followers do fewer, more intense sets
Cutting a bodybuilding program in half for the same results is impossible; minimalism produces unbalanced physiques
He works 55 hours a week and has a family, so he would cut training time if he could get the same gains; every set he does is there for a reason
Halving a 50,000 tonnage program loses 25,000 while halving a 10,000 powerlifting program loses only 5,000; equal percentage cuts hurt the maximalist far more
He enjoys lifting but does not let hedonism dictate training length; he does what is necessary and goes home
Lifters six feet and taller usually cannot ignore body parts and may need more work than shorter men for similar results
Training is rigid: he trains as planned regardless of whether he feels like it; taking a week off for lack of motivation is a dangerous mindset
Letting life dictate deloads may work for minimalist hobbyists with stressful lives, but he would regress because something comes up every week
He does not travel, stays home and lives like a sedentary monk, a lower-stress life than many
Total rest weeks are bad; neural adaptations detrain much faster than muscle, so after a break you waste weeks rebuilding before you can challenge the muscle again
Example: quads that can squat three plates may only manage about 255 lb after two weeks off, even though the muscle could still handle three plates
A minimalist cares about six or seven main lifts; he has about 25, so each week off neglects many more muscles and patterns
Size regresses slowly; the problem with time off is not lost muscle but lost performance and work capacity that must be rebuilt
Running does nothing for his muscles, so cardio is not a substitute for bodybuilding-specific training during a break
Size and strength are correlated, but whoever says so usually prioritizes strength; natural bodybuilders prioritize size with strength as the by-product
Strength athletes grow the muscles that drive their best lifts, e.g. Enkiri's legs and lats from squats and pull-ups, but have weak points like chest, biceps and the long head of the triceps
Twenty-rep squat widowmakers build more muscle than one-rep maxes because of greater tonnage, while daily heavy singles build more strength; rep range is the divide between size and strength
Picture size and strength as stacked columns: you grow the bottom one to raise the top one you care about, and which is on top depends on your priority
Enkiri is stronger on every lift, yet NH outweighs him by about 50 lb; focused purely on performance he could sit at 180-190 lb, but prioritizing size keeps him around 210
If every muscle were treated as a priority, a minimalist would end up training as much as he does
Optimally the recovery bucket is at 100% before training again, but 90% still leaves enough function to empty it; bodybuilders do not need peak performance
Small recovery shortfalls can accumulate into under-recovery; that is poor fatigue management that demands attention, so his method is not for novices
Deloading is only one way to clear fatigue; with squats on Tuesday and Friday, quad fatigue drops on Wednesday and Thursday even while you train other muscles
He programs muscle splits because they flush fatigue muscle by muscle, and a proper split also rests the CNS
Deload advocates suffer confirmation bias: they deload, never meet CNS fatigue, and credit the deload for preventing something that may never have come
Claiming tendons silently accumulate damage that deloads fix is self-contradictory: if tendon fatigue cannot be felt, you cannot know a deload avoided it
Deload weeks are a cop-out that stop lifters learning day-to-day fatigue management; a PR after a week off only shows full performance, not better long-term muscle building
Taking a week off every 6 or 12 weeks adds up to a lot of lost work over years; on a three-day schedule one missed day is about 30% of the week's training
Muscle building is simple: train the muscle, accumulate fatigue, rest, train it again; every muscle can grow that way
Novices should not deload; they need to learn fatigue management
Tendon pain that disappears after a deload often signals training that is too tendon-heavy and too light on the muscles; the deload is a band-aid, not a fix
Weekly deloads reset muscle, CNS and tendon fatigue to zero, hiding how these variables relate and wasting muscle stimulus
Bodybuilders should grow the CNS to serve the muscles, keeping it fresh enough to activate them, not manage muscles around the CNS as strength athletes do
Junk volume before a deload is not the deload's fault; likewise injuries from his method are poor fatigue management, not the method's fault
Programs should not be designed for the dumbest possible user; liability-driven restriction makes bad programs
Undulating load suits powerlifters who peak: a 400 lb deadlift at 80% is a building block toward a max; bodybuilders do not peak, so dropping intensity sacrifices for nothing
Bodybuilders should prioritize stability; strength work exists only to accumulate high-quality tonnage so other patterns can progress
Bodybuilding lost 50-60 years of methodological progress to steroid-driven pro methods and must emancipate itself from powerlifting
Size and strength programs can be told apart purely by numbers: rep ranges, exercise selection and frequency; most YouTube 'bodybuilding' programs read like powerlifting
A 10% loss returned quickly on one lift becomes huge when multiplied across six or more movement patterns, so breaks cost bodybuilders more
Autoregulate through sets and reps, not load: keep the weight fixed (e.g. 420 lb) and vary between three sets and one set of 4-8 reps, which manipulates tonnage just as well
Volume is the key variable to manipulate for bodybuilding and intensity is the key variable for powerlifting; neither ignores the others
He does deload, constantly, through set and rep management; 'I never deload' meant he does not deload the powerlifter way
'Gains happen when you rest' is a platitude; gains are triggered in training and materialize in recovery, and fatigue accumulation drives progression
Training is the number one priority; you can over-recover and miss stimulus windows, which wastes time
A deload gives absolute recovery, not optimal recovery; optimal recovery frequency means recovering as often as possible by juggling muscle buckets
Without accumulated fatigue a week off is detraining, not deloading; you can only deload from a load, and you can recover while still loading
Working smart exists to let you work hard; you can train smart without training hard, but you cannot train hard sustainably without training smart
He trains six days a week for hours, near maximal loads and to failure, which only works because his programming is smart
A powerlifter plateaus on a lift that is 80-100% of his pattern; for him the bench is about 20% of horizontal-press tonnage, so plateaus matter less and he cannot recall his last one
Many 'hard-training' bodybuilders really do junk volume and masochistic theatrics like 20-rep leg press until vomiting, which is garbage for hypertrophy
Michael Jordan was a workhorse who worked hard rather than smart
Most exercise science is designed around strength and function; applying it straight to hypertrophy is like a surgeon using veterinary studies
The fitness-fatigue model lumps strength and muscle into 'fitness' and muscle and CNS into one fatigue column, and ignores that bodybuilders need not be fully performant
Calling fatigue 'the bad stuff' demonizes it; without fatigue there is no fitness
Fatigue decays fast and fitness slowly, so chasing a pure fatigue flush risks lowering fitness; fatigue should be accumulated rather than flushed
His bodybuilding formula: performance minus fatigue equals fitness; performance only exists to let you accumulate fatigue
Bodybuilders should stay around 70-90% rather than maxing out, because maxing piles on fatigue quickly and forces a deload for minimal fitness
Powerlifters use fatigue management to drive performance; bodybuilders look for chances to perform so they can accrue fatigue
Minimalists favor undershooting fatigue; maximalists risk little by overshooting a bit but suffer if they undershoot, because their box of muscles is huge
Steroid users' huge programs exceed a natural's work capacity; copying them leads to burnout
His deload is built into every week via evolving reps, sets and rotations that slightly vary volume, intensity and frequency while keeping tonnage stable
exercises: about 20% of his horizontal-press tonnage; variations matter more
